approachQuestion.prompt:
Lab Benches
Each experiment occupies one bench during [start,end). Return the minimum number of benches needed to run all experiments at their given times. An experiment ending at time t may share a bench with one starting at t. Example: [(0,4),(2,5),(4,6)] → 2; [(1,2),(2,3)] → 1.

1 ≤ n ≤ 200000 intervals; integer 0 ≤ start < end ≤ 1000000000. Input is read-only and unsorted. Return only a count. Which approach best meets this contract?
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 200000 intervals; integer 0 ≤ start < end ≤ 1000000000. Input is read-only and unsorted. Return only a count.

options.text: Sort a copy by start time. Maintain a min-heap of ends of active experiments; before each start, remove every end at or before that start. Insert the new end and track the largest heap size.
options.feedback: The heap represents exactly the simultaneously active experiments after insertion. Their peak count is both a lower bound and achievable by reusing released benches.

options.text: Copy starts and ends into separate arrays, sort both, and sweep events while counting active experiments; process ends before starts at equal times. Return the maximum count.
options.feedback: This computes the same peak overlap with the same worst-case time and auxiliary space; end-before-start implements half-open intervals.

options.text: Use the start-ordered heap method but remove ends only when strictly less than the next start.
options.feedback: For [(1,2),(2,3)], the ended experiment would remain active and incorrectly require two benches.

options.text: For every start time, scan all intervals and count those containing it, then return the maximum count.
options.feedback: The count is correct because a new maximum begins at a start, but repeated full scans are avoidable.

details: Sort a copy by start time. Maintain a min-heap of ends of active experiments; before each start, remove every end at or before that start. Insert the new end and track the largest heap size.

Half-open experiments ending at the new start release benches before the arrival. Remove all expired ends, not only one. The largest active heap size measures required simultaneous benches rather than total experiments.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze A specifically: comparison-sort a copied interval array with iterative heapsort, then maintain a binary min-heap of active ends. Let n be interval count. Heap arrays have capacity n, and each record copy is constant-time. Choose the tightest time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Use the tightest worst-case bound for the whole input unless amortized or expected accounting is explicitly specified. Comparing or moving a record and arithmetic on machine words take constant time.

Exclude supplied input and returned output from auxiliary space. Count working arrays, queues, tables and call stacks. Output storage is separate and is not used as workspace. Heap repairs and traversals are iterative. No hashing is used unless explicitly stated.

options.text: O(n log(n+1)) time, O(n) auxiliary space
O(n log(n+1)) time, O(1) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Sorting and one heap lifetime per interval give the total bound.
details: Sorting costs O(n log(n+1)). Every interval is inserted once and removed at most once; heap work stays within that bound. The copied intervals and heap consume O(n) space, even though only a scalar answer is returned. Half-open equality changes correctness, not asymptotic cost.
“O(n) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: Unsorted starts must be ordered and active ends require heap repair.
“O(n log(n+1)) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: The copied intervals and active-end heap are workspace.
“O(n²) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: The inner purge loop removes each end once; it does not rescan every interval per start.
